blocks.text: KMP (Knuth Morris Pratt) is a string matching algorithm that finds every occurrence of a pattern inside a text in guaranteed O(n+m) time, no matter what the text or pattern contain.

That last part is the whole point. Naive matching can degrade to O(n*m) on unlucky inputs, and even Rabin Karp's average case O(n+m) can degrade to O(n*m) if hash collisions pile up. KMP never degrades. Its linear time bound holds for every input, every time.

items: Naive matching: on a mismatch, restarts the pattern comparison from scratch at the next position
KMP: on a mismatch, uses information it already gathered about the pattern to jump ahead intelligently, without ever re-examining a text character it has already looked at

blocks.text: This is achieved with a single precomputed array built once from the pattern itself, commonly called the LPS array or the failure function. It is what separates KMP from every simpler string matching approach.

Because KMP relies purely on comparing pattern characters against each other, never on any numeric mapping or hashing, it works identically on any alphabet, and its behavior is fully deterministic. The same pattern always produces the same LPS array, and the same input always takes the same number of steps, run after run.
The simplest way to find a pattern inside a text is to try every starting position and compare character by character.

For a text of length n and a pattern of length m, there are roughly n-m+1 starting positions, and each one can take up to m comparisons before a mismatch shows up. In the worst case, such as a text of a million as and a pattern of a thousand as followed by a b, nearly every position matches for a long stretch before failing at the very last character. That pushes naive matching to O(n*m).

The real flaw is not just the cost. It is what naive matching throws away. When a mismatch happens after nine characters have matched, naive matching forgets all nine and starts the next attempt from a blank slate, even though it already knows exactly what those nine characters were.

Patterns with internal repetition make this worse, not better. A pattern like "AAAAB" searched inside a text of mostly As forces naive matching to redo almost the same four character comparison at every single shifted position, since the partial match it just discarded looks almost identical to the one it is about to attempt again.
KMP is built entirely around fixing that one wasted piece of information.

content.title: 2. The Core Insight: Reuse What You Already Matched

blocks.text: When a mismatch happens partway through a match attempt, the characters that matched so far are not random. They are a specific prefix of the pattern, and that prefix has a fixed, known structure, since it is determined entirely by the pattern itself, not by the text.

KMP asks a question before the search even begins: for every prefix of the pattern, if a mismatch happens right after this prefix, how far back into the pattern can I safely resume without re-checking any text? The answer to that question, for every position in the pattern, is precomputed once into the LPS array.

This is why KMP's text pointer never moves backward, not even once, across the entire search. Every text character is looked at, and matched against the pattern, at most a small constant number of times.

blocks.caption: Naive matching restarts from scratch on a mismatch. KMP falls back the pattern pointer using the LPS array and never revisits a text character.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785249819095-639978627.png
blocks.alt: KMP core insight: text pointer never moves backward

blocks.text: KMP never re-examines a text character it has already looked at. Everything it needs to know about a partial match is already encoded in the pattern, not the text.

This also means KMP needs no hash function, no modulus, and no collision handling. The only tool it uses is direct character comparison, both while building the LPS array and while scanning the text, which is exactly why its worst case bound can be proven unconditionally rather than only on average.

content.title: 3. The LPS Array: Longest Proper Prefix Which Is Also a Suffix

blocks.text: LPS stands for Longest proper Prefix which is also a Suffix. A proper prefix or suffix means it cannot be the entire string itself, only a strict piece of it.
For a pattern of length m, the LPS array has one entry per index. Formally:

codes.javascript:
lps[i] = length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i]
         that is also a proper suffix of pattern[0..i]

blocks.text: A small example makes this concrete. For the pattern "AAAA":

items: lps[0] = 0 (a single character has no proper prefix)
lps[1] = 1 (for "AA", the prefix "A" equals the suffix "A")
lps[2] = 2 (for "AAA", the prefix "AA" equals the suffix "AA")
lps[3] = 3 (for "AAAA", the prefix "AAA" equals the suffix "AAA")

blocks.text: The value that matters most during a search is lps[j-1], where j is how many pattern characters had matched right before a mismatch. It tells KMP exactly how many of those already matched characters can be trusted to still be lined up correctly, so the pattern pointer can jump straight there instead of falling all the way back to index 0.

Not every pattern benefits equally. A pattern with no internal repetition at all, such as "ABCDE", has an LPS array of all zeros, so every mismatch falls the pattern pointer straight back to index 0, exactly like naive matching's restart. Even then, KMP still guarantees O(n+m), because the text pointer still never moves backward, only the pattern pointer resets, and that reset costs at most one step per mismatch.

content.title: 4. Worked Example: Building the LPS Array for ABABAC

blocks.text: Take the pattern "ABABAC" (indices 0 to 5). It has a repeating "ABAB" structure followed by a character, C, that appears nowhere else, which makes the fallback behavior easy to see clearly.
The construction keeps a running variable len, the length of the current matched prefix/suffix, starting at lps[0] = 0 and len = 0, and walks the pattern from i = 1 onward:

codes.javascript:
i=1: pattern[1]='B' vs pattern[len=0]='A'  -> mismatch, len=0 so lps[1]=0
i=2: pattern[2]='A' vs pattern[len=0]='A'  -> match, len=1, lps[2]=1
i=3: pattern[3]='B' vs pattern[len=1]='B'  -> match, len=2, lps[3]=2
i=4: pattern[4]='A' vs pattern[len=2]='A'  -> match, len=3, lps[4]=3
i=5: pattern[5]='C' vs pattern[len=3]='B'  -> mismatch, len!=0 so len=lps[2]=1
     pattern[5]='C' vs pattern[len=1]='B'  -> still mismatch, len!=0 so len=lps[0]=0
     pattern[5]='C' vs pattern[len=0]='A'  -> still mismatch, len==0 so lps[5]=0

Final LPS array: [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0]

blocks.caption: Building lps[5]: two consecutive fallbacks inside the LPS construction itself, using lps[len-1] each time, never resetting straight to 0.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785249821056-471385138.png
blocks.alt: LPS array construction for pattern ABABAC with double fallback at index 5

blocks.text: Index i = 5 is the interesting case. A single mismatch there triggers two fallback steps in a row, first to lps[2] = 1, then to lps[0] = 0, before finally landing on lps[5] = 0. This chaining is exactly what makes the construction subtle, and exactly what the next section's code has to get right.

content.title: 5. Constructing the LPS Array in C++

blocks.text: The construction is a self referential two pointer scan: the pattern is compared against itself to discover its own repeating structure.

The critical line is len = lps[len-1]. On a mismatch, it would be tempting to just set len = 0 and move on, but that throws away exactly the kind of information KMP is built to preserve. Falling back through lps[len-1] lets the scan try a shorter, already known prefix/suffix candidate without losing the progress made so far, which is exactly the chaining seen for ABABAC at index 5.

Notice i only ever increases in this loop. len can decrease, but only by jumping to a smaller value it already computed earlier. That single fact is what keeps this construction at O(m) instead of O(m^2).

This fallback logic is not unique to construction. The exact same x = lps[x-1] pattern reappears, unchanged, inside the main search loop in the next section. Once the fallback idea is understood here, the search algorithm has almost nothing new left to learn, only a second pointer into the text alongside it.

content.title: 6. The KMP Search: Two Pointers That Never Backtrack

blocks.text: With the LPS array ready, the search itself uses two pointers: i into the text, and j into the pattern, both starting at 0.

items: Characters match: advance both i and j by one
j reaches the pattern length: a full match ended at i-1, record it, then fall back j = lps[j-1] to keep searching for overlapping matches
Mismatch and j != 0: fall back j = lps[j-1], exactly like LPS construction, and try again without moving i
Mismatch and j == 0: there is nothing to fall back to, so simply advance i

blocks.text: Across all four cases, one guarantee never breaks: i is only ever incremented, never decremented. Every text character is examined a bounded number of times no matter how the pattern is structured, which is the entire reason the search phase runs in O(n).
Worked example: searching for ABABAC inside a longer text

codes.javascript:
text    = "ABABABCABABAC"   (indices 0..12)
pattern = "ABABAC"          lps = [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 0]

i=0..4  steady matches,               reaching i=5, j=5
i=5: text[5]='B' vs pattern[5]='C'    mismatch, j=lps[4]=3
i=5: text[5]='B' vs pattern[3]='B'    match,    i=6, j=4
i=6: text[6]='C' vs pattern[4]='A'    mismatch, j=lps[3]=2
i=6: text[6]='C' vs pattern[2]='A'    mismatch, j=lps[1]=0
i=6: text[6]='C' vs pattern[0]='A'    mismatch, j==0 so i=7
i=7..12 steady matches,               j reaches 6 at i=13

Match found starting at index 7 (i - j = 13 - 6 = 7)

blocks.text: Two things stand out. First, the fallback at i=5 is not wasted, since text[5] is B which immediately matches pattern[3], also B, so the very next comparison succeeds. Second, the double fallback at i=6 mirrors the exact same chaining seen earlier while building the LPS array, because both use the identical rule: fall back through lps[j-1] until either a match is found or j reaches 0. Notice i itself never once decreases, even while j falls back twice in a row.
Putting the LPS construction and the search loop together gives the complete algorithm.

When j reaches m, a full match has just been found ending at i-1, so it starts at i-j. Falling back with j = lps[j-1] right after recording it, rather than resetting to 0, is what lets KMP correctly find overlapping matches, such as every occurrence of "AA" inside "AAAA".

The final else branch, plain i++ with no change to j, only ever runs when j is already 0, meaning there was no partial match to protect in the first place. Every other mismatch is handled entirely through the LPS array, never through any special case tied to the alphabet or the specific text.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Phase","Time","Why"],"rows":[["Building the LPS array","O(m)","i only increases; len can fall back, but only to values it already computed"],["Searching the text","O(n)","i only increases across the entire search, every text character examined a bounded number of times"],["Total","O(n + m)","Guaranteed for every input, no dependency on pattern structure or text content"],["Extra space","O(m)","Just the LPS array itself, no space proportional to n"]]}

blocks.text: The reason the text pointer never backtracks is the crux of the whole algorithm. Naive matching backtracks the text pointer to try the next starting position from the beginning. KMP instead moves all of that backtracking into the pattern pointer, and only by amounts the LPS array has already precomputed, which is what turns an O(n*m) worst case into an O(n+m) guarantee.

The search phase deserves the same amortized argument as construction. Across the whole run, j increases by exactly one on every character match, and it can only fall back to a smaller value it already knows about. Since i increases at most n times total, the total amount j can ever increase is bounded by n too, which bounds the total number of fallback steps across the entire search, not just per character.

Unlike Rabin Karp, whose worst case depends on how the hash function behaves on a given input, KMP's O(n+m) bound holds unconditionally. There is no adversarial text or pattern that can push it past linear time.
Both algorithms solve the same single pattern search problem in average O(n+m) time, but they get there very differently, and that difference matters when choosing between them.

items: KMP: O(n+m) guaranteed worst case, no risk of hash collisions, but the LPS construction is fiddlier to get right and is built for exactly one pattern at a time
Rabin Karp: O(n+m) average case only, can degrade to O(n*m) under hash collisions, but the rolling hash idea is simpler to implement and generalizes naturally to searching for many patterns at once

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","KMP","Rabin Karp"],"rows":[["Worst case","O(n+m), guaranteed","O(n*m), under hash collisions"],["Core idea","Precomputed failure function on the pattern","Rolling hash compared before verifying characters"],["Best fit","Single pattern, hard guarantee required","Multiple patterns, duplicate substring detection"],["Extra risk","None, pure character comparison","Hash collisions if modulus or base chosen poorly"]]}

blocks.text: In an interview, KMP is the answer when the question emphasizes a worst case guarantee. Rabin Karp, or its generalization with a set of pattern hashes, is the answer when the question involves multiple patterns or duplicate substring detection.

Many interview problems do not mention string matching at all on the surface. They ask about a string's own repeating structure, its prefixes, or how it compares to its own reverse, and the LPS array turns out to be exactly the right tool underneath.
Common mistakes

items: Resetting len straight to 0 on a mismatch: instead of falling back through lps[len-1], this silently turns the construction quadratic and produces a wrong LPS array whenever a pattern has nested repeats, exactly like ABABAC above
Confusing the LPS array's own index with the pattern's index: lps[j-1] during the search refers to how far the pattern pointer j had advanced, not a position in the text
Off by one when reading lps[j-1] versus lps[j]: the fallback always uses the length just before the mismatched position, not the mismatched position itself
Forgetting to fall back after a full match: resetting j to 0 instead of lps[j-1] after recording a match silently skips overlapping occurrences
Moving the text pointer backward anywhere in the search: if i is ever decremented, the O(n) guarantee for the search phase is gone

blocks.text: Problem patterns

items: Easy Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String (LC 28): the canonical KMP problem, implement the search directly
Medium Shortest Palindrome (LC 214): build pattern = reverse(s) + "#" + s and read the last LPS value to find the longest palindromic prefix
Medium Repeated Substring Pattern (LC 459): a string is built from a repeating substring exactly when n % (n-lps[n-1]) == 0 and lps[n-1] > 0
Medium Longest Happy Prefix (LC 1392): the answer is simply lps[n-1] of the string itself, no search phase needed at all

blocks.text: KMP is the algorithm to reach for whenever a problem needs a hard guarantee on string matching time, or reduces to reasoning about a string's own prefixes and suffixes, not just its match against a separate text.
